commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][NIXL] Report a full prefix cache hit as finished
commits.pr_body:
Reopens #54714 (accidentally closed by a bad force-push that orphaned the branch history; GitHub would not let it reopen). Same single commit, with @njhill's review addressed: `awaiting_kvs` gating with tests for the abort seed and `num_external_tokens == 0` readback, plus the cosmetic comments (condensed comments, collapsed tuple assignment).

## Purpose

`_read_blocks` returns early when the local block list is empty — D already holds the KV, so only the producer needs telling — and it returns without recording anything. `get_finished` builds `done_recving` from `_recving_transfers` and `_failed_recv_reqs`, so the request is named in neither.

The scheduler has no other way to release it:

```python
if request.status == RequestStatus.WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS:
    if request.request_id not in self.finished_recving_kv_req_ids:
        return False
```

There is no timeout. The request stays in `skipped_waiting` — a queue counted in neither `num_running_reqs` nor `num_waiting_reqs` — holding the blocks it was allocated, for the life of the process.

Recording an empty transfer list is enough: `_pop_done_transfers` already treats a request with no outstanding handles as complete. This does it whether or not the notification lands, since the KV is local either way and a failed notification only costs the producer a timeout before it frees its own blocks, which is what the existing message says.

## How it showed up

A 10-prefill/3-decode deployment under saturation. Restarting peers made `send_notif` fail 122 times in half an hour, and each of those requests was abandoned. The three decode workers ended up holding 73–85% of their KV cache with zero running and zero waiting requests and no traffic anywhere on the deployment, until their liveness probes killed them. Only a restart cleared it.

The state is hard to see from outside: with the requests parked in `skipped_waiting`, both queue-depth gauges read zero while most of the cache is spoken for.

## Test Plan

`test_full_prefix_cache_hit_is_reported_finished`, parametrised over the notification succeeding and failing, asserts the request reaches `done_recving`.

## Test Result

Against the unpatched worker the request is reported in neither case; patched, in both.

commits.pr_title: [Model][DSv4.1] Store the whole KV in MXFP8 (FlashMLA V4.1 record)
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

DeepSeek-V4.1 has been reusing DeepSeek-V4's paged `fp8_ds_mla` record. FlashMLA has a V4.1-specific one that quantizes the RoPE dims too; this switches DeepSeek-V4.1 onto it on SM100.

| | V4 (`ModelType::V4`) | **V4.1 (`ModelType::V41`)** |
|---|---|---|
| data row | 448 B fp8 e4m3 NoPE + 128 B bf16 RoPE | **512 B fp8 e4m3, RoPE included** |
| scale row | 7 UE8M0 of 64 dims + 1 pad byte | **16 UE8M0, one per 32 dims (MXFP8)** |
| bytes/token | 584 | **528** |
| page (TMA) stride | 576 B | **512 B** |

Both records put a page's whole data region ahead of its whole scale region, so a page is `block_size * bytes_per_token` rounded up to the TMA stride. Because `block_size` is always a multiple of 32, every V4.1 page is an exact multiple of 512 — the padding the V4 record needed disappears, on top of the 9.6% smaller record.

Gated on SM100: `ModelType::V41` is absent from FlashMLA's SM90 sparse-decode feature set, so SM90, ROCm and the FlashInfer SM120 path keep the V4 record. No new cache dtype and no new flag — `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` resolves to `fp8_ds_mla` as before and the record follows the arch, exactly as `fp8_ds_mla` already means 656 B for V3.2 and 584 B for V4.

### What changed

- **FlashMLA pin** → `vllm-project/FlashMLA@b6ef01c`, following the fork's tree reorganization (`csrc/sm*` → `csrc/kernels/sm*`, API implementations split into `.cpp` files). `api.cpp` now registers `fused_norm_rope_attn_rope_cast_*` and the two permute kernels, so their instantiations must be compiled for `_flashmla_C` to link; the source list mirrors the fork's `setup.py` minus the dense backward, which is training-only.
- **Writers**: the fused SWA insert takes a `kv_mxfp8` argument (one UE8M0 scale per lane pair instead of per four, and the RoPE lanes quantize instead of storing bf16); the compressed-cache insert gets an MXFP8 kernel that applies RoPE *before* choosing scales, since the RoPE dims are now quantized.
- **Readers**: the Triton gather and the CuteDSL gather are parameterized by record instead of hard-coded to 448/64, and both pick it from `k_cache.shape[-1]` — the per-token width the KV cache spec already publishes — so the V4 record keeps working unchanged on the same code path.

### The indexer page has to move with them

`_get_bytes_per_block` makes a block's stride the **sum** of every page in the group, and DeepSeek-V4/V4.1 packs the SWA cache, the compressed-KV cache, the indexer cache and the compressor ring into one block. Divisibility by the TMA stride therefore only holds if *every* contributing page carries the same padding — which is what the indexer cache's 576 B alignment was for, rather than any constraint of its own kernel.

Leaving the indexer at 576 while the main caches moved to 512 produced a block stride of 212160 (a multiple of neither) and tripped FlashMLA's `block_stride_bytes % TMA_K_STRIDE == 0` assertion in the startup profile run, after a clean weight load. Every per-spec page size looked correct in isolation. This PR ties the indexer's alignment to the same gate.

## Relationship to other open PRs

- **#56344 (`[Perf] Deepseek V41 Attention MegaKernel`, same author)** integrates FlashMLA PR #221's fused norm+RoPE+attention megakernel behind `--attention-config '{"dsv4_fused_attention": true}'` and adds an `nvfp4_ds_mla` dtype pairing a 528 B SWA cache with a 288 B fp4 compressed cache. This PR is the narrower, unconditional half: it moves DeepSeek-V4.1's *existing* `fp8_ds_mla` cache to the V4.1 record with no opt-in and no new dtype, and it does not touch the attention path. The two overlap on `flashmla.cmake` (that one pins `c112cc1`, this one `b6ef01c` — one commit later, a test-only change in the fork) and on the V4.1 writers/readers; whichever lands first, the other rebases onto it. #56344 does not currently touch `DeepseekV4IndexerCache.get_kv_cache_spec`, so the alignment fix above is worth carrying across either way.
- **#56441 (`[Perf][DSpark] Add KV-only context insertion across V4.1 cache formats`)** touches the same three `csrc/libtorch_stable/` files to add a KV-only wrapper op. The changes are disjoint in intent (its wrapper drops the dummy query; this adds a record selector) but will conflict textually on the op signature and bindings.

Not duplicating either: neither makes the V4.1 MXFP8 record the layout DeepSeek-V4.1 actually runs with by default, and neither carries the indexer-alignment fix.

## Test Plan & Result

```
pytest tests/kernels/test_compressor_kv_cache.py \
       tests/kernels/test_fused_deepseek_v4_qnorm_rope_kv_insert.py   # 271 passed, 11 skipped
pytest tests/v1/attention/test_sparse_mla_backends.py                 # 392 passed, 378 skipped
pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_flashmla.py \
       tests/kernels/attention/test_flashmla_sparse.py                # 10 passed, 144 skipped
pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_cache.py -k mla \
       tests/model_executor/layers/test_mla_short_prefill_indexer.py \
       tests/kernels/test_cp_gather_fp8.py                            # 97 passed, 12 skipped
pytest tests/v1/worker/test_dsv4_packed_zeroer_geometry.py \
       tests/v1/attention/test_indexer_deepseek_v4_slot_mapping.py    # 20 passed
pre-commit run --files <changed files>                                # all hooks pass
```

Three new tests cover the record: a byte-exact check of the compressed-cache insert against a reference quantizer derived from FlashMLA's `tests/quant.py`, an insert→gather round trip (which also exercises the CuteDSL path), and the CUDA op's MXFP8 branch against the Triton encoder.

## Model evaluation

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (revision `517ef625`), TP4 on one GB300, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8 --block-size 128 --max-model-len 65536`, no speculative decoding. Baseline is the same weights/TP/node on the V4 584 B record.

| task | V4 record (584 B) | **V4.1 MXFP8 (528 B)** |
|---|---|---|
| gsm8k, greedy 5-shot completions, n=1319 | 0.9272 / 0.9310 | **0.9333** flexible · **0.9340** strict |
| gpqa_diamond, thinking, T=1.0 | 0.904 / 0.899 (epoch 1) | **0.9028** (epoch 4, n=792) · pass@4 0.9495 |

0 request errors on both. GPQA truncated 3/792 rows; answered-only accuracy 0.9062. Quantizing the 64 RoPE dims costs nothing measurable.

Comparability caveat: the baselines were taken with the `deepseekv41-flash-0909` image at gpqa `epoch_num: 1`, this run with a local build at `epoch_num: 4`, so the arms differ in image and epoch count as well as in the record. The gsm8k arm at temperature 0 is the tight comparison and it is clean.

Engine-level evidence beyond the scores: FlashMLA hard-errors on any byte count that is not 584/528/288 for `d_qk=512`, so a clean startup — memory profiling, KV allocation (161.73 GiB, 11,589,848 tokens) and full CUDA-graph capture of the sparse decode path — is itself proof the 528 B record was accepted as `ModelType::V41`.

## AI assistance

This change was developed with AI assistance (Claude Code). The FlashMLA pin bump, the record change across the writers/readers, the indexer-alignment fix, the new tests and the evaluation runs above were produced in that session and reviewed by me.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Handle bare and malformed tool call openers in Gemma4 parser
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Fixes #53431.

`gemma-4-26b-a4b-it` emits tool calls in multiple formats beyond the documented `<|tool_call>call:name{...}<tool_call|>`:

1. **Bare opener**: `<|tool_call>:name{...}<tool_call|>` — omits `call`
2. **No brace**: `<|tool_call>call:name prose<tool_call|>` — no opening `{`
3. **Round bracket**: `<|tool_call>call:name(args)<tool_call|>` — uses `(` instead of `{`

The parser FSM had no transition for any of these, causing the tool call to be **silently dropped** (case 1) or the `function.name` to **absorb everything after it** including the closing token and subsequent well-formed tool calls (cases 2, 3). The latter was reported by @chriskosys in the issue discussion.

## Root cause

`gemma4_config()` in `vllm/parser/gemma4.py` defines:
- Only `CALL_PREFIX` (`"call:"`) as the transition from `TOOL_PREAMBLE` to `TOOL_NAME` — bare `:` opener never matches.
- Only `OPEN_BRACE` (`"{"` ) as the transition from `TOOL_NAME` to `TOOL_ARGS` — if the model never emits `{`, the FSM is stuck in `TOOL_NAME` (which emits `TOOL_NAME` events), swallowing the closing `<tool_call|>` and all subsequent content into `function.name`.

## Fix

Two changes:

1. **Bare opener**: Add `COLON` (`":"`) terminal with `(TOOL_PREAMBLE, "COLON") -> TOOL_NAME` transition.

2. **Escape hatch**: Add `(TOOL_NAME, "TOOL_END") -> CONTENT` transition so any malformed call that never produces an opening brace is bounded to itself. The closing `<tool_call|>` returns the FSM to `CONTENT`, emitting `TOOL_CALL_END`, so subsequent content and tool calls are processed normally.

The lexer matches longer literals first, so `"call:"` (5 chars) still takes priority over `":"` (1 char) — no behavior change for existing outputs. Colons in content or argument values are unaffected.

## Verification

### Before fix (5 scenarios)

| Scenario | `function.name` (before) | Second call recovered? |
|----------|--------------------------|-----------------------|
| `call:search_files prose<tool_call\|>` | `search_files prose<tool_call\|>` | N/A |
| `call:bad_func no brace<tool_call\|>` + `call:get_weather{...}` | `bad_func no brace<tool_call\|><\|tool_call>call:get_weather` | No |
| `:bad_func no brace<tool_call\|>` + `call:get_weather{...}` | `bad_func no brace<tool_call\|><\|tool_call>call:get_weather` | No |
| `call:terminal(command:...)<tool_call\|>` | `terminal(command:...)<tool_call\|>` | N/A |
| `call:terminal(...)<tool_call\|>` + `call:get_weather{...}` | `terminal(...)<tool_call\|><\|tool_call>call:get_weather` | No |

### After fix

| Scenario | `function.name` (after) | Second call recovered? |
|----------|------------------------|-----------------------|
| `call:search_files prose<tool_call\|>` | `search_files prose` | N/A |
| `call:bad_func no brace<tool_call\|>` + `call:get_weather{...}` | `bad_func no brace` + `get_weather` | **Yes** |
| `:bad_func no brace<tool_call\|>` + `call:get_weather{...}` | `bad_func no brace` + `get_weather` | **Yes** |
| `call:terminal(command:...)<tool_call\|>` | `terminal(command:...)` | N/A |
| `call:terminal(...)<tool_call\|>` + `call:get_weather{...}` | `terminal(...)` + `get_weather` | **Yes** |

### Test results

| Test suite | Tests | Result |
|-----------|-------|--------|
| Existing gemma4 parser tests | 54 | ✅ All pass |
| Bare opener edge cases | 7 | ✅ All pass |
| Colon stress tests | 17 | ✅ All pass |
| TOOL_NAME escape tests | 9 | ✅ All pass |
| **Total** | **87** | **✅ Zero regressions** |

## Tested environment

- NVIDIA RTX PRO 5000 × 8 (Blackwell, SM120, 72GB each)
- vLLM 0.27.1, Python 3.10

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][KV Offload] Ignore pending chunks in invalid sliding windows
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

A pending CPU KV write can unnecessarily defer a request even when an earlier sliding window is ready to load. For a two-chunk window, `[HIT, HIT, MISS, HIT_PENDING]` currently returns `None`: the reverse scan keeps the pending flag after the miss has already ruled out that incomplete suffix. The core scheduler therefore submits no load for the ready prefix.

Track pending writes within the current consecutive window and clear that state when a miss invalidates the window. A pending chunk inside a usable window still defers lookup, and `RETRY` retains its existing conservative behavior. No timeout, transfer ownership, or external API changes are introduced.

## Why this is not duplicate work

I checked #49829 and #53087 discussions and searched open PRs for `_sliding_window_lookup`, `HIT_PENDING gap`, and related offload/window/defer terms on 2026-09-11. #53087 addresses bounded waits, #53330 addresses P2P supply/demand coverage, and #51787 addresses cache recency. This change fixes the stale pending flag for an already-invalid sliding window. It does not claim to fix the production stalls reported in #49829 or an underlying stalled transfer.

## Test Plan

The regressions fail against the unchanged base: the scanner returns `None`, and the real core scheduler plus CPU manager submits zero loads. With the fix, both synchronous and asynchronous scheduling load the earlier prefix and resume the remaining prompt while the unrelated CPU write is still pending.

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector/test_scheduler.py \
```

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Export weight-cache IPC tensors separately for each client
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Starting a copy-mode client can release the weight cache while another engine is still using zero-copy weights. The daemon currently calls `reduce_tensor` once and sends the same arguments to every client. Those arguments include a reference-count slot for one consumer, so releasing the copy client's temporary IPC tensors can bring the count to zero while the other engine still holds its mappings.

Export the tensors for each `get_state` response instead. PyTorch then tracks each consumer separately and can keep the underlying allocation alive after the daemon drops its model. Exporting at startup is removed as well, so there is no unused initial reference. The request protocol stays the same.

Related: #51259 fixed export reuse in packed weight transfers; this change covers the separate weight-cache daemon. I checked the related Fast Start PRs, including #56047 and #55468, and found no existing fix for this path.

This change and its tests were developed with AI assistance.

## Test Plan

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/model_executor/model_loader/test_weight_cache.py \
  -k ipc_cache_release_keeps_live_consumers -v

.venv/bin/pre-commit run --files \
  vllm/model_executor/model_loader/weight_cache/daemon.py \
  tests/model_executor/model_loader/test_weight_cache.py

.venv/bin/pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --hook-stage manual --files \
  vllm/model_executor/model_loader/weight_cache/daemon.py \
  tests/model_executor/model_loader/test_weight_cache.py
```

The CUDA multiprocessing regression covers copy-only and mixed zero-copy/copy clients. It checks that releasing the daemon cache keeps the producer allocation alive for a live zero-copy consumer, that consumers can still read their tensors, and that the allocation is reclaimed after the last consumer exits.

commits.pr_title: [KVConnector][P2P] Configurable unbound-store timeout and one-RTT rejection of a late fetch
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Fixes the two problems reported in #53128 for the `p2p` secondary offloading tier.

A producer parks a request's stored KV blocks until the consumer's `FetchMsg` binds them to a
session, and reaps them after 60 s so they stop pinning primary-tier CPU slots.

1. **The 60 s ceiling was not configurable.** Deployments whose prefills legitimately run
   longer than that had no recourse. This adds an `unbound_store_timeout_s` tier config key,
   defaulting to the existing 60 s, shaped like the tier's other keys (`host`, `port`,
   `backends`, `num_threads`) — i.e. per-tier, documented, and validated:

   ```bash
   --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"OffloadingConnector","kv_role":"kv_both",
     "kv_connector_extra_config":{"spec_name":"TieringOffloadingSpec",
       "secondary_tiers":[{"type":"p2p","unbound_store_timeout_s":180}]}}'
   ```

2. **A fetch arriving after the reap was never rejected** — this is the user-visible damage.
   `_poll_once` bound the id to the session and `ServerRole` parked demand that no
   `submit_store` could ever satisfy, so the consumer burned its full
   `_LOAD_TIMEOUT_S` (30 s) plus an abort round trip before falling back to local prefill.
   Reaped ids now go into a time-pruned `_reaped_stores` map and `_poll_once` finalizes the
   round on the spot, so the peer receives `TransferDoneMsg(success=False)` on the same tick
   and recomputes immediately. No protocol change and no new session API — this reuses the
   existing `finish_request` → `_finalize_outbound` terminal path.

Where the reap clock starts (first vs. last stored chunk) is deliberately left alone: the
reporter measured only ~6 s of spread when idle and ~13 s under load, which is not what makes
the failure painful.

As a side effect this removes a real leak. The reap path's `self._failed_req_ids.add(kid)` was
documented as making "a late inbound `FetchMsg` short-circuit to a clean rejection", but no
code on the fetch path ever read that set, so the claim never held; and because the producer
request had already run `on_request_finished` (the only `discard` site), the id was never
removed and the set grew for the lifetime of the process.

## Not a duplicate

- **#53235** adds an `unbound_store_timeout_s` knob via an undocumented `kwargs.pop` and
  nothing else. The knob alone leaves the 30 s consumer stall in place, which is the actual
  regression; its PR body also misdescribes the change ("keep it until it is safely
  bound/consumed" — it parameterises the reap, it does not remove it). This PR carries both
  halves of the fix and shapes the knob as documented, validated tier config.
- **#52912** is referenced by the issue but addresses a different area.

## Test plan

```
venv/bin/pytest tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/p2p/test_manager.py -v   # 69 passed
venv/bin/pytest tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/p2p/ -v                 # 207 passed
pre-commit run --files vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/p2p/manager.py \
  tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/p2p/test_manager.py \
  docs/features/kv_offloading_usage.md                              # all hooks pass
```

New test `test_late_fetch_after_reap_fails_immediately` asserts the *path*, not just the
outcome: the consumer's load job completes with `success=False`, **no `AbortFetchMsg` ever
crosses the wire** (proving it came from `TransferDoneMsg`, not the timeout-then-abort path),
and elapsed wall clock is far below `_LOAD_TIMEOUT_S`. Verified that the test fails on the
unpatched manager — the consumer gets no result at all within the bounded poll count.

The existing `test_unbound_store_reaped_after_timeout` was updated for the `_failed_req_ids`
→ `_reaped_stores` move.

No model eval: the change affects only failure-path timing and a config default, never
generated output.

## AI assistance

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to write this change. I reviewed every changed line and
ran the test commands above myself.

Closes #53128

commits.pr_title: [ROCm][DSv4.1][Perf] Dequantize the MXFP8 weight once when dot_scaled cannot be used
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

`RocmDotScaledMxfp8LinearKernel` needs `K % 128 == 0` for `tl.dot_scaled`. Where that does not hold, `apply_weights` dequantizes the weight instead:

```python
w_bf16 = dequant_mxfp8_to_bf16(layer.weight, layer.weight_scale)
out = torch.nn.functional.linear(x2d, w_bf16).to(x.dtype)
```

`layer.weight` and `layer.weight_scale` are constant after loading, so that rebuilds the same tensor on every forward. This converts it once in `process_weights_after_loading` and keeps BF16 — what `EmulationMxfp8LinearKernel` already does under `VLLM_MXFP8_EMULATION_DEQUANT_AT_LOAD` — and has `apply_weights` dispatch on the weight's element size.

## Why it is worth a patch

`dequant_mxfp8_to_bf16` is six pointwise kernels, and its FP32 intermediate is 4x the FP8 source and round-trips through HBM twice, so a 2.95 MB weight costs 56 MB of traffic.

On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash it fires on one linear per layer, and which one depends on TP: `moe_intermediate_size` is 2304, and the shared expert's `down_proj` is row-parallel, so its K is sharded while `gate_up`'s stays at 5120.

| TP | down_proj K | `K % 128` | path |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | 2304 | 0 | dot_scaled |
| 2 | 1152 | 0 | dot_scaled |
| **4** | **576** | 64 | **dequantize** |
| **8** | **288** | 32 | **dequantize** |

TP1 and TP2 never see this; TP4 and TP8 pay it on all 40 layers — 2.24 GB of HBM traffic per decode token to produce 236 MB of weights that never change.

## Test Plan

4x MI355X (gfx950), ROCm 7.2.3, TP4, on `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly-eed1f3d0c6043bd494424a22443ee198dd56f657`. Server as the recipe composes it — `--tokenizer-mode deepseek_v41 --tensor-parallel-size 4 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 --moe-backend aiter_triton_mxfp4_bf16`, `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1`, `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_MOE=1` — with `cudagraph_mode=FULL_DECODE_ONLY` pinned, and a fresh server per arm.

```bash
vllm bench serve --backend vllm --model /model \
  --served-model-name DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash --dataset-name random --ignore-eos \
  --random-input-len 8192 --random-output-len 1024 \
  --max-concurrency {1,8} --num-prompts {8,24}
```

The board drifts between processes, so the unpatched arm was run both first and last.

## Test Result

| arm | median TPOT, c=1 | median TPOT, c=8 |
|---|---:|---:|
| unpatched, first | 10.60 ms | 12.34 ms |
| **patched** | **10.10 ms** | **12.05 ms** |
| unpatched, last | 10.57 ms | 12.33 ms |
| | **-4.6%** | **-2.3%** |

The two unpatched arms are 0.28% apart at c=1 and 0.08% at c=8, so the effect is 16-29x the drift over that span.

A decode profile confirms the mechanism rather than inferring it from the timing: `exp2_kernel_vectorized4` and `CUDAFunctorOnSelf_add<float>` go from 2600 calls each to **exactly zero**, and `bfloat16_copy_kernel_cuda` from 2665 to 65 (the remainder is an unrelated once-per-step collapse). Weight memory rises 0.11 GiB per rank, which is the 236 MB of BF16 predicted from the weight shapes less the 118 MB of FP8 it replaces.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Carry over queued work when materializing the dedicated stream
commits.pr_body:
# Carry over queued work when materializing the dedicated stream

## Purpose

`vllm.utils.torch_utils.current_stream()` is a getter that *mutates* the current
stream: the first call per thread runs
`torch.cuda.set_stream(torch.cuda.Stream())`. Nothing ties the new stream to the
one it replaces. Pool streams are created with `cudaStreamNonBlocking`
([`c10/cuda/CUDAStream.cpp`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/c10/cuda/CUDAStream.cpp):
`constexpr unsigned int kDefaultFlags = cudaStreamNonBlocking;`), so there is no
implicit ordering with the default stream either. Work already enqueued before
the switch and work issued after it are therefore unordered: a consumer on the
new stream can read a tensor whose producer is still pending on the old one.

Whether the first call happens before any device work is enqueued is decided by
runtime config, not by construction. On the common CUDA path it is early —
pynccl's `_init_communicator` calls `current_stream()` before its warmup
`all_reduce`, and cudagraph capture calls it too — but those are the only things
pinning it. With a distributed backend that does not go through pynccl and
`--enforce-eager`, the first call landed in
`fused_moe/runner/shared_experts.py`'s `self._stream.wait_stream(current_stream())`,
inside the first MoE layer of a warmup forward: the sequence-parallel
`input_ids` produced immediately before stayed on the old stream while MoE
routing consumed them on the new one, reading unwritten bytes and routing on
garbage token ids.

The fix makes the new stream `wait_stream()` the one it replaces. The switch
still happens (the dedicated stream is required for cudagraph capture); this
adds a single cross-stream dependency, once per thread, at a point where the
process is switching streams anyway. No steady-state cost: `current_stream()`
takes the fast path after the first call, and deliberate overlap via
`with torch.cuda.stream(...)` is untouched.

## Not a duplicate

`gh` was unavailable in my environment, so the duplicate check was done through
the same queries via the GitHub search API:

- `is:pr is:open wait_stream` → 6 results: #53997, #51349, #47355, #51117,
  #29288, #45452. All add or move *deliberate* side streams, or fix an unrelated
  CPU-side race; none touch the lazy first switch inside `current_stream()`.
- `is:pr is:open "current_stream" stream ordering` → #53782, #41834, unrelated.
- `is:pr torch_utils current_stream dedicated`, `is:pr "first call" set_stream`,
  `is:issue is:open current_stream race` → 0 results.
- `git log -- vllm/utils/torch_utils.py` shows no prior attempt at this ordering.

## Test plan and results

Hardware disclosure: I have no NVIDIA GPU available. Verification was done on a
vendor accelerator whose platform reports `PlatformEnum.CUDA` and which goes
through this exact branch, so the code path under test is the one being changed,
but **the CUDA-hardware runs still need to come from CI or a reviewer.**

1. Targeted repro of the hazard (single device, `--enforce-eager` equivalent):
   dirty a 256 B block and free it → back up the stream in use with 200 chained
   2048² bf16 matmuls → reproduce the `reorder_token` `index_select` that
   allocates that block → call `current_stream()` (the switch) → read the tensor
   on the new stream with no explicit sync, then run the routing kernel.

   ```
   before: stream 0x0 -> 0x565543daba10  switched=1 stale=1 routed_ok=0
           truth=[0, 1, 2, 3, 60, 61, 62, 63]
           peek =[2816, 2817, 2818, 2819, 2820, 2821, 2822, 2823]
   after:  stream 0x0 -> 0x562057893010  switched=1 stale=0 routed_ok=1
           peek == truth, routing correct, two consecutive runs identical
   ```

   `switched=1` in both arms: the change makes the switch safe rather than
   avoiding it.

2. Real model, TP8, `--enforce-eager`, MoE model with the shared-experts runner:
   with the switch left wherever it lands by default, 13 of 20 warmups faulted
   with out-of-window device reads or silently mis-routed. Forcing the first
   `current_stream()` call into worker init — a vendor-side change that moves the
   switch out of the forward, *not* this patch — made warmup clean and
   completions correct. That run establishes the mechanism and where the first
   call lands; the effect of *this* patch is established by (1).

3. Lint: `ruff check vllm/utils/torch_utils.py` → `All checks passed!`;
   `ruff format --diff` → `1 file already formatted` (ruff 0.14.10).

Not run by me, and worth asking CI for: any CUDA test that exercises cudagraph
capture plus multi-stream overlap, e.g. `tests/compile/` and the
`tests/distributed/` pynccl tests, to confirm the extra dependency changes
nothing on the paths where the switch already happens at init.

## Model evaluation

The change is an ordering fix only; it adds no numerics. On the affected
configuration it turns a silent mis-routing / fault into correct output. No
accuracy delta is expected on configurations where the switch already happens
before any queued work (i.e. everything using pynccl or cudagraph capture),
which is why I did not run a separate eval sweep — say the word if you want one
on a specific config.

## AI assistance

This change was developed with AI assistance (Claude Opus, via a CLI agent):
the root-cause analysis, the patch, and the repro script were produced in that
session and reviewed line by line by me before submission. I understand the
change and can defend it in review.

## Purpose

Fix incorrect pooling outputs when Model Runner V2 uses pipeline parallelism and a request spans multiple scheduler steps. `Worker.execute_model()` previously called `pool()` only when the model forward returned `None`; non-final PP ranks instead return `IntermediateTensors`, so their pooling post-step never advanced `num_computed_tokens`. commits.pr_body:
# Context
Currently, adaptive verification is only enabled for DSpark speculators that have a confidence head. This PR enables it for ALL draft-model-based speculator types (MTP, EAGLE3, DFlash 1&2), including DSpark when a confidence head is not available.

NOTE: The attention backend(s) of the base model must still support variable length verification, which is the existing prerequisite for DSpark adaptive verification. This PR depends on #52992, which extends that support to the backends used here (Inkling sconv / rel-attention, FLASH_ATTN, FLASH_ATTN_MLA); all benchmarks below were captured with it applied.

# This PR

This PR implements an online acceptance estimator that learns to predict acceptance probabilities for draft tokens using the draft's logits. Adaptive verification now works for DFlash, DFlash2, MTP, and any other draft-model speculator, provided that the attention backend(s) of the base model supports variable length verification.

The feature used is `logit(max q)`, the log-odds of the draft distribution's most likely token.

# Results Summary

Adaptive verification OFF vs ON, output token throughput, mean of two passes per arm with both arms in one session. temp 1.0 / top_p 0.95, concurrency 64, <=2K in / 2K out, natural EOS.

| model | hardware | draft depth | accept len (OFF) | mean tok/s gain |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MiMo-V2.5-Pro-FP4 + DFlash | 4xGB200 | 8 | 1.9 – 5.1 | **+19.0%** |
| Inkling-NVFP4 + MTP8 | 4xGB200 | 8 | 2.3 – 4.2 | **+17.6%** |
| Kimi-K2.5 + DFlash \* | 8xH200 | 8 | 2.8 – 4.4 | **+44.5%** |
| Muse-Glimmer-30B + DFlash2 | 1xGB200 | 7 | 2.7 – 4.7 | **+14.7%** |

\* Kimi-K2.5 was run separately on 8xH200 over gsm8k / humaneval / mt-bench only (no speed-bench). The Blackwell rows are five datasets each.

Per dataset, every one improves. The gain tracks how far drafts overrun acceptance: within a model the biggest wins are on speed-bench high-entropy (**+34.0%** on MiMo, **+32.3%** on Inkling, where the target accepts under 2.4 of 8 drafted tokens), and across models the largest is Kimi-K2.5, whose very high per-token verification cost makes each trimmed token worth more.

## Versus a trained confidence head

**DeepSeek-V4-Flash + DSpark** is shipped with a confidence head, so natually was used as a baseline to compare the estimator with.

| evidence | estimator | trained head |
|---|---|---|
| held-out AUC, 1.4M graded drafts | **0.8228** | 0.8224 |
| held-out ECE (calibration) | 0.0087 | **0.0076** |
| held-out log-loss | **0.4435** | 0.4472 |
| tok/s, probabilistic | **+2.1%** | — |
| median TPOT, probabilistic | **-3.8%** | — |
| accepted/drafted, probabilistic, 5 datasets | **+4.06pp** on 5 of 5 | — |
| tok/s / TPOT, greedy | -0.6% / +0.3% (tie) | — |

- **AUC (Area Under the Curve)**: The probability that a randomly chosen accepted draft scores above a randomly chosen rejected one (0.5 = chance). Computed by the Mann-Whitney rank-sum identity, verified against brute-force pair counting. Measures discrimination.
- **ECE (Expected Calibration Error)**: bins predictions and compares each bin's mean predicted probability against the frequency actually observed, weighted by bin occupancy — so 0.0087 means predictions are off by ~0.9pp on average. Measures calibration.
- **log-loss**: The mean negative log-likelihood of the predicted acceptance probability, so it penalizes confident wrong answers and rewards calibration.
- Generated-token counts match across arms to within 0.4–4.3%, making `tok/s` a relatively stable way to compare performance.

### Takeaways:
- Greedy is a tie on every metric, with signs disagreeing across datasets: the estimator matches the trained head without needing one.
- Estimator has slightly better AUC and log-loss compared to the confidence head => slightly better discrimination.
- Confidence head has slightly better ECE (expected calibration error) => better calibration.
- Estimator has slightly better tok/s, and lower TPOT => better performance.

Interestingly, the estimator's better discrimination comes from the deeper draft positions:
| draft position | estimator AUC | head AUC | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| k=0 | 0.7956 | **0.8313** | −0.0356 |
| k=1 | 0.8107 | **0.8160** | −0.0053 |
| k=2 | **0.8273** | 0.8148 | +0.0125 |
| k=3 | **0.8391** | 0.8124 | +0.0267 |
| k=4 | **0.8494** | 0.8098 | +0.0396 |

The confidence head clearly leads on the first position, but the estimator pulls ahead during the deeper positions.

# How it works

For each drafted token the estimator fits a per-position logistic regression

```
p_accept(k) = sigmoid(w * logit(max q) + b[k])
```

where `max q` is the draft model's probability of its most likely token, `w` is a slope shared across draft positions, and `b[k]` is a per-position intercept. Both are refit continuously during serving.

**Prediction happens during draft sampling.** `sample_draft` already materializes the draft logits in order to draw a token, so the estimator scores the same rows in the same pass. Every draft-model speculator routes through that one call site, which is why MTP, DFlash and EAGLE3 need no speculator changes. Only DFlash2, which samples through a selector walk rather than `sample_draft`, scores at its own equivalent point.

The probability is written into two index spaces at once: the persistent request-state slot, where the next step's refit will find it alongside the label the target eventually produces, and the current batch position, which is what adaptive verification indexes by. Keeping both avoids a reorder later, since the batch is compacted between the two uses.

**Trimming reuses the existing adaptive verification path unchanged.** The estimator only supplies the per-position probabilities that DSpark's confidence head previously supplied. `record_confidences` publishes them and starts an async device-to-host copy, `get_num_tokens` sizes the global draft budget on CPU from the landed copy, and `_assign_draft_token_budget` ranks every `(request, step)` slot on device by its **survival probability** (the running product of that request's per-position confidences) admitting the globally best `draft_budget` slots. Because survival only decreases along a request, a global top-k always admits a prefix of each request's drafts, so `compact_batch` and `reallocate_drafts` can shorten the verification batch without any per-request bookkeeping.

**Per step**, `propose()` folds the previous step's drafts (now graded accepted or rejected by the target) into IRLS sufficient statistics, and every `REFIT_INTERVAL` steps solves for new coefficients. Because the slope is shared by all draft positions, the information matrix is an arrowhead and the solve collapses to a scalar equation, so no per-position matrix inverse is needed.

**Updates are damped by sample count.** Newton steps are scaled by `n / (n + DAMPING_OBSERVATIONS)`, but the slope and the intercepts count different things. The slope learns from every position, so it is damped by the round's total across all of them and is effectively undamped at serving batch sizes. Each intercept is damped by its own position's count, and observations thin out with depth because a deep position only exists when the shallower ones were accepted and admitted, so deeper `b[k]` move more conservatively, and a position nobody reached in a round has `n = 0` and holds still.

# Why `logit(max q)`

**Losslessness is the reason.** The more obvious candidate is `logit(q_sampled)`, the log-odds of the token the drafter actually drew, and it fits the data better than anything else evaluated here (0.8463 AUC / 0.4221 log-loss, in the table below), clear of both `logit(max q)` and the trained head. It was tested but later rejected because it introduces selection bias (not lossless).

Scoring the *drawn* token makes the trim decision a function of that token, so the drafts surviving to verification are no longer distributed as `q` while rejection sampling still corrects with `min(1, p/q)`. The emitted distribution tilts toward the drafter's confident modes. A two-token counterexample: `q = (0.9, 0.1)`, `p = (0.5, 0.5)`, verify only if `q(x) >= 0.5` — the output is `a` with probability 0.55 against a true 0.50.

`max q` is a function of the draft distribution, hence of the prefix alone. The admission decision for position `i` is therefore fixed before `x_i` is drawn, no subset of `x_i` is selected against, and the rejection sampler's precondition holds.

Held-out fit quality on ~1.4M labelled drafts (DeepSeek-V4-Flash + DSpark), mean of 5 random splits (sd <= 0.0008 on every row):

| drafting | feature | lossless | AUC | log-loss |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| probabilistic | top-2 margin | yes | 0.8043 | 0.4576 |
| probabilistic | entropy | yes | 0.8226 | 0.4787 |
| probabilistic | **`logit(max q)`** | **yes** | **0.8228** | **0.4435** |
| probabilistic | margin + `logit(max q)` | yes | 0.8273 | 0.4404 |
| probabilistic | *trained confidence head* | *yes* | *0.8224* | *0.4472* |
| probabilistic | `logit(q_sampled)` | **no** | 0.8463 | 0.4221 |
| probabilistic | `-log(-log q_sampled)` | **no** | 0.8473 | 0.4200 |
| greedy | **`logit(max q)`** | **yes** | **0.8758** | **0.3632** |
| greedy | top-2 margin | yes | 0.8712 | 0.3651 |

Takeaways:
- **`logit(max q)` beats the trained confidence head** on log-loss (0.4435 vs 0.4472) and ties it on AUC, while costing no trained weights.
- **The rejected candidates score higher.** `logit(q_sampled)` and `-log(-log q_sampled)` reach 0.8463 / 0.8473 AUC, about 0.024 above the best lossless feature. That gap is the price of correctness, and it is not payable: those scores are only reachable by conditioning on the drawn token, which is what breaks the sampler's precondition.
- **Discrimination is not calibration.** Entropy ranks as well as `logit(max q)` (0.8226 vs 0.8228 AUC) but is far worse calibrated (0.4787 vs 0.4435), and the allocator consumes probabilities. This predicts the reported failure of an entropy-based score elsewhere, where keep-ratio collapsed 0.689 -> 0.522.
- **Under greedy the distinction disappears.** The drawn token *is* the argmax, so the two candidates are the same quantity. Only probabilistic drafting is at risk.

**Shared slope, per-position intercepts.** The slope does nearly all the work. On the same held-out split, per-position intercepts alone score 0.5941 log-loss; adding the shared slope against a single global intercept takes that to 0.4474, and splitting the intercept per position takes it to 0.4433 — so the slope contributes 0.1467 of the 0.1508 total and the per-position intercepts add the remaining 2.7%. Sharing the slope is what makes deep draft positions usable: they see too few observations per round to fit two parameters, but an intercept alone is well determined.

## Fitted coefficients across models

| model | drafting | nspec | samples | slope `w` mean | `w` sd | intercept `b[k]` mean | `b[k]` sd |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash + DSpark | probabilistic | 5 | 35 | 0.5013 | 0.0250 | -0.137 | 0.208 |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash + DSpark | greedy | 5 | 38 | 0.6482 | 0.0371 | -0.551 | 0.125 |
| MiMo-V2.5-Pro-FP4 + DFlash | probabilistic | 8 | 69 | 0.5145 | 0.0458 | -0.923 | 0.114 |
| Muse-Glimmer-30B + DFlash2 | probabilistic | 7 | 67 | 0.4426 | 0.0337 | -0.158 | 0.245 |
| Inkling-NVFP4 + MTP8 | probabilistic | 8 | 85 | 0.5859 | 0.0349 | -0.614 | 0.142 |
| Kimi-K2.5 + DFlash | probabilistic | 8 | 21 | 0.8261 | 0.0629 | -0.234 | — |

`b[k]` is averaged over draft positions, so both its columns match the slope's: the mean is over positions and refits, the sd is across refits. Kimi's per-refit coefficients were not published, only its per-position means, so its sd is unavailable. Averaged the other way (across positions rather than refits) the spread is 0.077–0.238, so within a model the intercepts sit close together and it is their common level that moves between models.

The slope is **stable within a model** (per-dataset sd 0.013–0.046, CV ~5%) but **shifts across models and drafting modes** (0.44 to 0.83). The intercepts absorb dataset difficulty: on DSV4 `b[0]` swings from +0.66 on easy stretches to -0.65 on speed-bench high-entropy while `w` barely moves.

# Robustness

The estimator was stress-tested against the trained head on the axes where an online fit should degrade and a frozen one should not: temperature away from 1.0, a single pooled slope spanning clients at different temperatures, and a hard distribution shift mid-serving. **It matched or beat the head on every one.** All figures below were measured on `logit(max q)`.

**Temperature.** Accepted/drafted, estimator minus head, two reps per condition:

| condition | est - head | run-to-run spread | |
|---|---|---|---|
| uniform temp 0.6 | -0.51pp | 0.86pp | inside |
| uniform temp 1.5 | +0.51pp | 1.99pp | inside |
| mixed batch, 0.6 client | +0.17pp | 1.12pp | inside |
| mixed batch, 1.5 client | -0.02pp | 0.64pp | inside |

The mixed rows are the case a single pooled slope should handle worst: two concurrent clients 2.5x apart in temperature share one batch and one slope. Both land inside their own noise, the high-temperature client at -0.02pp.

**Hard bidirectional distribution shift, no restart.** The fit is converged on low-entropy temp 0.6, then the workload swings to high-entropy temp 1.5 and back, twice, without restarting the server. Two measured windows per phase:

| window | estimator a/d | head a/d | gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| B1 — first window after shifting to high-entropy | 22.06% | 19.57% | **+2.49pp** |
| B2 — second window, same phase | 21.86% | 20.91% | +0.95pp |
| A1 — first window after shifting back to low-entropy | 50.36% | 47.27% | **+3.09pp** |
| A2 — second window, same phase | 47.49% | 47.39% | +0.09pp |

Adaptation lag would show up as the *first* window after a shift trailing the second. It does not: the estimator's first windows are its strongest (-0.20pp and -2.88pp going from first to second), and it leads the frozen head in all four. With rounds carrying ~10k observations the damping factor is ~0.995, so a refit is nearly a full Newton step and the fit tracks the new regime within 1-2 rounds (100-200 engine steps).

Caveats: two reps per temperature condition and one measured window per shift phase, all on a single checkpoint. The head arm was noisier in this run than the estimator (its uniform-1.5 spread is 1.99pp against the estimator's 0.27pp), which widens the bar "inside spread" has to clear, so the temperature result is partly a statement about a loose noise floor rather than a tight match.

# GSM8K Accuracy Eval - adaptive verification OFF vs ON

Paired design: same 1319 GSM8K questions and the same per-request seed in both
arms, temp 1.0 / top-p 0.95 / top-k 20, concurrency 64, 4096-token cap, natural
EOS. Pairing lets McNemar's exact test run on the discordant answers, which is
far more sensitive at n=1319 than comparing two independent accuracy rates.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash + DSpark | 5 | 1319 | 93.93% | 93.40% | -0.53pp | 26 / 19 | 0.371 | 0 / 0 | 16 |
| Muse-Glimmer-30B + DFlash2 | 7 | 1319 | 96.29% | 96.21% | -0.08pp | 11 / 10 | 1.000 | 0 / 0 | 7 |
| Inkling-NVFP4 + MTP8 | 8 | 1319 | 95.98% | 95.83% | -0.15pp | 6 / 4 | 0.754 | 0 / 0 | 24 |
| MiMo-V2.5-Pro-FP4 + DFlash | 8 | 1319 | 95.83% | 96.29% | +0.45pp | 11 / 17 | 0.345 | 0 / 0 | 20 |
| **POOLED (all four)** | | **5276** | **95.51%** | **95.43%** | **-0.08pp** | **54 / 50** | **0.769** | **0 / 0** | |

No significant change in accuracy from enabling adaptive verification with the acceptance estimator.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Redact credentials from benchmark logs
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

`vllm bench serve` printed its full argument namespace, including values passed through `--header`, while the multi-turn benchmark logged both `--api-key` and `--header`. This could expose credentials in local or CI logs. The fix uses one small shared helper to log a sanitized copy while leaving the original arguments unchanged for requests. The same sanitized copy is used for optional PyTorch benchmark metadata so credentials are not moved from stdout into an artifact.

## Reproducer

```bash
PATH="$PWD/.venv/bin:$PATH" .venv/bin/vllm bench serve \
  --model unused \
  --dataset-name random \
  --num-prompts 1 \
  --header 'Authorization=Bearer redaction-test' \
  --max-concurrency 0

PATH="$PWD/.venv/bin:$PATH" .venv/bin/python \
  benchmarks/multi_turn/benchmark_serving_multi_turn.py \
  --input-file unused.json \
  --model unused \
  --api-key multi-api-redaction-test \
  --header 'Authorization=Bearer multi-header-redaction-test' \
  --warmup-percentages invalid
```

The deliberately invalid final arguments stop both commands immediately after their startup diagnostics, without sending a request.

## Output on **main** vs on **branch**

### Main

```text
... header=['Authorization=Bearer redaction-test'], max_concurrency=0 ...
... api_key='multi-api-redaction-test', header=[('Authorization', 'Bearer multi-header-redaction-test')] ...
```

### Branch

```text
... header='***', max_concurrency=0 ...
... api_key='***', header='***' ...
```

The original parsed values remain unchanged and are still passed to the HTTP request path.

## Test Plan

```bash
# Deterministic checks for serve stdout, PyTorch metadata, multi-turn logs,
# and preservation of the original Namespace values.
PATH="$PWD/.venv/bin:$PATH" .venv/bin/python -c '<redaction assertions>'

PATH="$PWD/.venv/bin:$PATH" .venv/bin/pre-commit run --files \
  vllm/benchmarks/lib/utils.py \
  vllm/benchmarks/serve.py \
  benchmarks/multi_turn/benchmark_serving_multi_turn.py

PATH="$PWD/.venv/bin:$PATH" .venv/bin/pre-commit run --all-files

PATH="$PWD/.venv/bin:$PATH" .venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/benchmarks/test_serve_cli.py -q --disable-warnings --tb=short
```

Results:

- Serve stdout redaction and argument passthrough: passed.
- Serve PyTorch artifact redaction and argument passthrough: passed.
- Multi-turn startup redaction: passed.
- File-scoped pre-commit: passed.
- Full pre-commit: all non-dependency hooks passed.

commits.pr_title: [ROCm][DSV4.1][Perf] Fold the mHC post step into the delayed pre projection
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on AMD runs an mHC post block and then the next sublayer's pre block at every seam. AITER can apply the post step and project the resulting residual in one kernel (`mhc_fused_post_pre_gemm_sqrsum`), which removes one launch per seam.

`deepseek_v4/amd/model.py` already reaches that kernel through `MHCFusedPostPreOp`. V4.1 could not, for the same reason it could not use AITER's plain `mhc_pre`: it collapses each sublayer's input with the **previous** sublayer's pre-mix, and AITER's fused entry point neither returns a pre-mix nor accepts an incoming one.

Builds on #56503, which has landed, so this is now a single commit against `main`.

## Approach

The post step is three optional arguments on the delayed-pre path that #56503 introduced, not a second op stack. Pass `sublayer_out` with its two mixes and the driver runs the fused projection; omit them and it runs the plain pre exactly as before. Everything after stage 1 is shared and untouched:

1. `mhc_fused_post_pre_gemm_sqrsum` — post step, plus the split-k projection and row square-sums of the new residual. This is the only stage the fusion changes; without it, `mhc_post` and `mhc_pre_gemm_sqrsum` run separately.
2. `mhc_pre_big_fuse` — post/comb gates and all Sinkhorn iterations.
3. `mhc_pre_mix_triton` — recovers this sublayer's pre-mix from the same unreduced GEMM output.
4. `hc_collapse_triton` — collapses the residual with the *incoming* pre-mix.

The post block's new residual is returned through a caller-allocated buffer (`mutates_args=["residual_out"]`) rather than as an op result, so the unfused path never has to hand back one of the op's own inputs. It replaces a buffer the driver used to allocate internally, so this costs no extra allocation.

## Where it does and does not fuse

- **Attention seam** — always fuses.
- **Seam after an Engram injection** — cannot fuse, because Engram reads the residual between the post and the pre. Falls back to separate ops.
- **Above 1024 tokens on gfx950** — falls back, mirroring AITER's own `fused_m_upper_bound`. Worth being explicit about why, since the name is misleading: `mhc_fused_post_pre_large_m` is *not* a fused kernel, it is plain `mhc_post` + `mhc_pre` with a non-temporal store hint (`store_nt=0`) and `large_m_splitk=True`, neither of which the fused kernel can express. Once the residual no longer fits in cache there is nothing left for fusion to save, so this is a decode-path optimization by construction.

## Test plan

`tests/kernels/test_mhc_kernels.py`:

- `test_mhc_fused_post_pre_delayed_rocm_aiter` — both seam variants (carried and absent pre-mix) across 1/2/7/128 tokens, against `mhc_post_torch` + `mhc_pre_delayed_torch`.
- `test_mhc_fused_post_pre_delayed_falls_back_for_large_batches` — pins the dispatch heuristic.
- `test_mhc_pre_delayed_rocm_aiter` — extended to assert that with no post requested the residual comes back unchanged, so the added argument cannot silently perturb #56503's path.

## Test result

MI355X (gfx950, 256 CU), TP4, `hidden_size=5120`, `hc_mult=4`, 20 Sinkhorn iterations. Launches are per seam, excluding the TP all-reduce.

| tokens | separate | fused | path |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5 | **4** | fused |
| 6 | 5 | **4** | fused |
| 24 | 5 | **4** | fused |
| 96 | 5 | **4** | fused |
| 1024 | 5 | 5 | unfused (AITER heuristic) |
| 2048 | 5 | 5 | unfused (AITER heuristic) |

On accuracy, the question is not the gap to an fp32 reference but whether fusing moved the result relative to the separate kernels it replaces. It differs by at most 3.6e-3 relative to tensor max, which is one bfloat16 ULP (2^-8 = 3.9e-3) on a bfloat16 residual — two accumulation orders rounding differently. Both paths sit the same distance from the fp32 reference. On the fallback path the outputs are bit-identical.

### End to end

Concurrency 1, 40 layers × 2 seams, so 80 launches removed per forward step.

The effect is small enough that it is not resolvable by serving one lane after another, so this is a **two-way crossover**: each arm is measured on both halves of an 8-GPU node with the same fixed 24-request replay at `--random-seed 42`. All eight cells emitted an identical 16141 output tokens, so the work is the same throughout. The crossover is necessary rather than fussy — the two GPU sets on this host differ by 0.96%, which is the same order as the effect being measured, and a single-orientation A/B put the answer anywhere from +0.3% to +2.2% depending on which half the fused lane happened to land on.

| | mean ITL |
|---|---|
| separate post + pre | 6.9015 ms |
| fused | 6.8141 ms |

**1.28% lower inter-token latency**, 95% CI [0.07%, 2.48%] (t = 2.94 on 4 df). At a 24 ms forward step that is 0.31 ms over 80 removed launches, or about 3.8 µs each, which is the right order for a ROCm launch on this host.

### Accuracy

gsm8k, all 1319 samples, greedy, CUDA graphs on:

| | strict | flexible |
|---|---|---|
| Torch mHC baseline | 0.9704 ± 0.0047 | 0.9697 ± 0.0047 |
| #56503 (delayed pre only) | 0.9727 ± 0.0045 | 0.9719 ± 0.0045 |
| this PR | 0.9735 ± 0.0044 | 0.9727 ± 0.0045 |

## Known follow-up

The fallback here is the *plain* post plus delayed pre, so it picks up neither of AITER's large-m tunings. That is inert between 1024 and 2048 tokens (`store_nt` flips above `8 * num_cu` and `get_mhc_pre_splitk_large_m` only diverges at 8192) but it is a real miss at prefill, which reaches 16384 tokens here. Wiring it needs a `store_nt` argument on the shared `mhc_post` wrapper that V4 also uses, so it is better as its own change.

Part of #56506, which also records why this and a fused all-reduce + mHC post are alternatives rather than additive: both consume the same post step.

commits.pr_title: [CI] Check target branch freshness before starting CI
commits.pr_body:
Outdated CI configuration can make a PR fail before its code is evaluated. Before `/ci run` or `/amd-ci run` creates a Buildkite build, check that the requested PR commit contains every current commit on its upstream target branch. This includes `all` and `nightly`, release branches, and stacked PRs.

- If the branch is behind, report its lag and ask the contributor to merge or rebase onto the latest target branch, then rerun the command.
- Allow `--allow-stale` on run commands with the same authorization requirements and an explicit warning about outdated CI configuration.
- Reject requests if freshness cannot be checked or the PR changes during the check. Use the existing workflow token without modifying PR branches.
- Document run-command freshness in contributor guidance and CI authorization notifications, and explain the separate repository settings needed to enforce merge requirements.


AI assistance from OpenAI Codex was used for the implementation, tests, and split.

commits.pr_title: [ROCm][DSV4.1][Perf] Stride the DSA decode candidate mask over the live context
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

`rocm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits` sizes its logits workspace as `(batch_size * next_n, max_model_len)` and hands the whole tensor to `apply_candidate_mask`, so the mask grid was sized by `max_model_len` rather than by the context actually resident. On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with `--max-model-len 1048576` that is 1024 programs per row when only the first ~128 have anything to do.

The cost tracked row count and ignored context, which is the signature of a grid sized by the workspace instead of the data. On gfx950 at block size 8, 2048 candidate blocks:

| rows | mask kernel |
|---:|---:|
| 6 | 0.0127 ms |
| 24 | 0.0357 ms |
| 96 | 0.1252 ms |

96 rows is 402 MB of stores in 0.1252 ms, i.e. the kernel writes the entire workspace every call regardless of sequence length.

Sanitizing columns at or past a row's `end` is dead work. `top_k_per_row_decode` bounds its scan by `rowEnd`, taken from the same `seq_lens` passed to the mask. That invariant is already load-bearing upstream: when there are no candidate blocks the mask is skipped entirely and top-k reads the same uncleaned workspace.

This replaces the one-program-per-tile grid with a fixed 128 programs that stride to the row's `end`. The grid is still derived from `width`, a tensor shape, so a FULL cudagraph capture stays valid on replay; only the loop trip count is data-dependent, and it is read from device memory inside the kernel rather than baked at capture. `min(_MASK_GRID_COLS, cdiv(width, 1024))` keeps narrow widths from launching programs that would only fall through, so the grid never grows relative to today.

### Why this sits next to the ROCm caller instead of replacing the shared kernel

An earlier revision of this PR changed `apply_candidate_mask` in `model_executor/kernels/attention/dsa/candidate_blocks.py` directly. The clamp itself is sound on every platform — `persistent_topk` takes `min(lengths[row], stride, max_seq_len)` and `cooperative_topk` passes its clamped `sl` into `large_topk`, so neither reads past `end` either, and the CUDA path allocates the same `max_model_len`-wide workspace.

The program count is the problem: 128 is a tuning constant measured against gfx950's 256 CUs, and I have no way to measure the tradeoff on NVIDIA. Rather than ship an unmeasured grid change to CUDA users, the variant lives beside its only caller in the ROCm ops file and the shared kernel is untouched. The four ROCm call sites are not equivalent either — the prefill chunks pass chunk-sized logits, where there is nothing to win, so they stay on the shared kernel and only the paged decode path switches.

Part of #56506.

## Test Plan

`tests/kernels/attention/test_rocm_aiter_candidate_mask.py` (new, ROCm-gated) is the unit test. Correctness is the load-bearing part, since the change deliberately stops writing to part of the tensor. Output must be bit-identical to the shared kernel over `[0, end)` for every row — the region a consumer can read — across the shapes that exercise the edge cases:

- ragged per-row ends, including 0, 1, tile boundaries (1023/1024/1025) and values up to 524287
- `end == width`, the only configuration where the edge flag at column `width - 1` is inside the compared region
- non-zero `starts` from the prefill path
- `row_repeat > 1`, where several logit rows share one bound
- `block_size` 16 as well as the model's 8
- widths either side of `_MASK_GRID_COLS * _MASK_TILE`, so both the saturated grid where programs actually stride and the `min()` clamp below it are covered
- a column stride > 1, since the caller slices a workspace

Two properties beyond agreement also get pinned: that columns past the tile boundary containing `end` are left untouched (the difference from the shared kernel, and where the speedup comes from), and that a cudagraph capture replays correctly against ends both longer and shorter than the captured ones — the property the static grid exists to provide.

Performance measured two ways: a standalone kernel benchmark at decode shapes over a range of contexts and grid widths, and in-situ torch-profiler decode traces on a live server at concurrency 1, 4 and 16, comparing per-kernel ms/step against an otherwise identical baseline. Accuracy via gsm8k 5-shot under lm-eval on the same node and configuration.

Hardware: MI355X (gfx950, 256 CU), TP4, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, `--max-model-len 1048576`, `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` cudagraph mode, DSpark 5-token MTP.

## Test Result

Correctness: 9 passed. All cases agree bit-for-bit over `[0, end)`.

To confirm the test is not vacuous, two mutations of the kernel were checked: stopping one tile early (`while tile_start < end - TILE`) and removing the stride (`step = TILE`, so programs never advance past their own tile span). Each fails 8 of the 9 tests; the one that still passes in both cases is the tail-bound test, which correctly does not constrain under-masking.

Standalone kernel, 131k context:

| conc | rows | before | after | speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 6 | 0.0128 ms | 0.0125 ms | 1.03x |
| 4 | 24 | 0.0356 ms | 0.0127 ms | 2.81x |
| 16 | 96 | 0.1236 ms | 0.0201 ms | 6.16x |

Across contexts at 96 rows: 32k 0.1249 -> 0.0125 (9.9x), 131k 0.1249 -> 0.0197 (6.3x), 524k 0.1464 -> 0.0786 (1.9x). The 524k case is where the kernel starts doing real work rather than padding, which is the intended behaviour. A grid clamped to the visible length — not capture-safe, measured only as a floor — gives 0.0192 ms at 131k, so the strided form is within 4% of the best a data-dependent grid could do.

In-situ decode traces, 4 mask calls per step, per-kernel ms/step:

| conc | before | after | speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 0.048 | 0.018 | 2.7x |
| 4 | 0.133 | 0.031 | 4.3x |
| 16 | 0.464 | 0.077 | 6.0x |

Reproduced to three decimals across two independent trace runs.

At concurrency 16 the whole-trace kernel delta is -0.404 ms/step and -0.387 of that is this kernel, with every other kernel inside ±0.04 ms, so the win is attributable rather than drift. The indexer chain goes from 2.95 to 2.58 ms/step, 11.4% to 10.0% of the decode step.

gsm8k 5-shot, lm-eval, same node and configuration:

| | strict-match | flexible-extract |
|---|---:|---:|
| baseline | 0.9719 ± 0.0045 | 0.9712 ± 0.0046 |
| this change | 0.9727 ± 0.0045 | 0.9719 ± 0.0045 |

That run predates the move out of the shared kernel, so it exercised this kernel on both the prefill and decode call sites — a superset of what the PR now changes.

One caveat worth stating rather than hiding: at concurrency 1 and 4, step wall time is dominated by variance in `cross_device_reduce`, which absorbs TP rank arrival skew and moved by more than 2 ms/step between runs that differ only in this file. End-to-end wall time at low concurrency cannot resolve an effect this size; the per-kernel attribution above is the measurement that can.
